name: Frequency Bands Directive (GSM)
impact_assessment: none (pre-dates impact assessments); 2007 repeal proposal COM(2007) 367
evidence_rating: thin: two older econometric diffusion studies (mixed on the value of a single mandated standard); no ex-post evaluation
summary: The 1987 GSM Directive reserved the 900 MHz band for one pan-European digital mobile system. Research shows the move to digital mobile drove rapid phone take-up in Europe, but a worldwide study found no extra diffusion boost from mandating a single digital standard. The rule was relaxed in 2009 to allow 3G, with forecast savings of up to EUR 1.6 billion that were never checked.

indicators.objective: The 1987 proposal predates financial statements with indicators; no monitoring indicators or review clause were set

indicators.indicator: Reserve 890-915/935-960 MHz for a single pan-European digital system (GSM) so terminals and networks work across borders
indicators.evidence: GSM became the dominant world standard; cross-country econometric work finds the analogue-to-digital switch (with more spectrum) had a major effect on EU mobile diffusion, but a single mandated digital standard had no significant extra effect on diffusion compared with competing standards elsewhere.

indicators.indicator: Opening the 900 MHz band to UMTS and later technologies (Directive 2009/114/EC)
indicators.target_or_baseline: Industry capital savings up to EUR 1.6bn (Commission estimate)
indicators.evidence: Not evaluated ex post; the figure is a Commission forecast reported in the trade press.

literature.citation: Gruber & Verboven (2001), The evolution of markets under entry and standards regulation - the case of global mobile telecommunications, International Journal of Industrial Organization 19(7) (CEPR DP 2440)
literature.title: The evolution of markets under entry and standards regulation - the case of global mobile telecommunications
literature.venue: International Journal of Industrial Organization 19(7) (CEPR DP 2440)
literature.method: econometric diffusion model, panel of countries 1981-1997 (not a clean causal design)
literature.headline: Setting a single standard significantly sped up diffusion for analogue mobile, but not for digital; network benefits of one standard appear offset by gains from competition between digital systems; adding competitors had a strong immediate effect
literature.summary_plain: A worldwide study found that imposing one standard helped analogue mobile spread, but the single digital standard (as with GSM in Europe) brought no measurable extra boost.

literature.citation: Gruber & Verboven (2001), The diffusion of mobile telecommunications services in the European Union, European Economic Review 45(3)
literature.title: The diffusion of mobile telecommunications services in the European Union
literature.headline: Transition from analogue to digital in the early 1990s, with the increase in spectrum capacity, had a major impact on diffusion; competition also significant; late-licensing countries catch up
literature.summary_plain: Across the EU, the switch to digital mobile (GSM) and the extra spectrum it brought were the main drivers of mobile phone take-up in the 1990s.
literature.quality: correlational; cannot separate the Directive from the technology

literature.citation: European Commission (2007), Proposal for a Directive repealing Council Directive 87/372/EEC (GSM Directive), COM(2007) 367
literature.title: Proposal for a Directive repealing Council Directive 87/372/EEC (GSM Directive)
literature.method: ex-ante (CEPT technical studies; no quantified IA in the text)
literature.headline: Reserving 900 MHz exclusively for GSM blocks more advanced systems such as UMTS; the band's propagation allows cheaper coverage of rural areas; CEPT found UMTS can coexist with GSM
literature.summary_plain: By 2007 the Commission saw the GSM-only rule as a barrier and proposed opening the band to 3G, citing cheaper rural coverage.

literature.citation: Telecoms.com (2009), EU move lends helping hand to UMTS900, trade press
literature.title: EU move lends helping hand to UMTS900
literature.headline: Commission expected industry savings of up to EUR 1.6 billion from reforming the GSM Directive (amended by Directive 2009/114/EC)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected opening the GSM band to 3G to save operators up to EUR 1.6 billion in network costs.
